did_you_know.text: The Sages later called the mitzvah described here bikkurim, or first fruits. The word “first” emphasizes bringing God the first and finest part of the harvest.
The phrase “An Aramean sought to destroy my father” is ambiguous. It can also be understood as “My father was a wandering Aramean.”
In the Bible, “honey” does not always mean bees’ honey; it can also mean a sweet syrup, such as date syrup. Thus, “a land flowing with milk and honey” describes agricultural abundance.
The tithe of the third year is known in Jewish tradition as the “poor person’s tithe.” It was meant to provide food for Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows within the community.

The verbs in verses 17–18, “you have affirmed” and “He has affirmed you,” are rare in Biblical Hebrew, so translations vary slightly. All the interpretations emphasize a mutual relationship between the people and their God.

In Biblical Hebrew, segulah means a treasured possession or special treasure, not magical power. This special status is presented together with the responsibility to be a holy people and keep the commandments.
